title: A hymn in Sarang
hookLine: Parmanand asks what all your listening has done, and Surdas says whose company to leave

lines: WHAT HAVE YOU DONE, BY LISTENING?
cards: What have you done, by listening? That's roughly the question that opens today's hymn, and it's a sharp one in a series where every day has asked you to listen.
A person sits through the holy stories, hears them told and retold, nods along. Then the hymn asks: and what came of it?
It's by the Bhagat Parmanand, one of the voices the Gurus set inside the Sarang section of the Guru Granth Sahib. Near it stands a short verse under the name of Surdas.

teach.h: WHAT HAVE YOU GAINED FROM HEARING?
teach.b: Here's Parmanand's hymn, in paraphrase. O man, what have you gained from hearing the Puranas told? Steady devotion hasn't welled up in you, and you haven't given to the hungry.
Lust hasn't left you, and neither has anger. Greed hasn't let go. You haven't stopped slandering others.
Then, in its closing line, the hymn names the company of the holy. Notice the target. Not the stories; Parmanand doesn't say a word against them.
It's the listener who hears and stays the same.

teach.h: NO DEVOTION, NO FOOD FOR THE HUNGRY.
teach.b: In the hymn, hearing is supposed to go somewhere: into devotion that holds steady, and into food on a hungry person's plate. If it goes nowhere, the hymn asks what it was for.
Surdas's verse makes a matching point from the other side.
In paraphrase: O mind, leave the company of those who have turned their backs on the Lord. Parmanand says hearing alone won't change you. Surdas says the people around you will, one way or the other.
Together they picture a devotion that isn't only an ear. It's hands and feet and the people you sit with. Now set it in Sarang, the midday raga.

Midday is lunchtime, the hour when someone who has listened all morning finds out whether any of it reached their hands: whether someone hungry gets fed, whether the slander at the lunch table gets joined or left.
That's the line for today: midday devotion.

how: The Bhagats' hymns in Raga Sarang, Parmanand's among them, are sung in kirtan beside the Gurus' own, and Sikhs join hearing the Word with seva such as serving food in the langar.

games.q: what does “a hymn in sarang” mean?
o: Parmanand's praise for hearing the holy stories every day
Parmanand's question: what has all your listening changed?
a midday prayer said before sharing the gurdwara's meal

games.q: what's inside the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: what have you gained from hearing?
leave the company of the turned-away

s: Parmanand's hymn speaks against the holy stories
it never criticizes them; it questions the listener who hears and stays the same.
the hymn names giving to the hungry as a sign of real listening
it says steady devotion hasn't welled up, and you haven't given to the hungry.
Surdas's verse is about choosing your company
O mind, leave the company of those who have turned from the Lord.

games.q: you've listened to holy stories all morning. at lunch, someone starts slandering a coworker. what does Parmanand's hymn point to?
o: join in; the listening was this morning.
let the hearing reach your hands and tongue.
go back and listen to more stories.
games.why: the hymn asks what hearing gained you if slander, greed and anger stay, and if the hungry go unfed.

practice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Sarang, or sit in the quiet, and ask yourself Parmanand's question without judging: of all the good things I've heard lately, what has reached my hands?

Let one answer come, even a small one, then one thing your hands could do today, a meal shared, a kind word in place of a sharp one, and just hold it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath; if you don't, simply breathe.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Sarang. Parmanand's question to the person who hears the holy stories and doesn't change, with Surdas's verse beside it about the company you keep. Today's word.

orig.note: bhagat: devotion; Parmanand asks why steady devotion hasn't welled up.

carryVoice: Your line: midday devotion. In Parmanand's hymn, listening is meant to reach the hands. See you tomorrow.
